title: Food and the code
hook: the code forbids ritually slaughtered meat; many Sikhs are vegetarian, others not

segments.voice: Yesterday, kara and kangha: a steel circle at the wrist and a comb in the hair. Your line was touch and remember. Before what act did you touch your wrist? Day one thousand two hundred ninety-one.

Two Sikh households, same street, same gurdwara, same Sunday. In one kitchen, there hasn't been meat in the house for as long as anyone can remember; the grandmother says it simply isn't their way. In the other, there's chicken on the stove for dinner. On Sunday morning both families sit side by side in the langar hall and eat the same meal: dal, a vegetable dish, roti, and a sweet. Nobody at the table asks what's waiting at home. What does the Sikh code actually say about food? Less than some expect, and the little it says matters.
screen: `TWO KITCHENS, ONE STREET.` → `THE SAME LANGAR MEAL.` → `WHAT DOES THE CODE SAY?`

segments.voice: First, the line the code does draw. Among the things an initiated Sikh must never do, the code names eating kutha: meat from an animal killed by ritual slaughter. Sikhs explain it in more than one way. Some see it as refusing to take part in another community's rite. Others see it as one piece of the Sikh refusal of empty ritual. Either way, it is a firm line. Second, what the code leaves open. It does not say every Sikh must be vegetarian. So Sikhs differ. Some keep a vegetarian kitchen, and some groups within the panth hold to it strictly and with deep feeling. Others eat meat that is not kutha. Both families on that street can be keeping the code. Third, the shared table. The langar serves vegetarian food, so that anyone, whatever their own rules about food, can sit and share it. The Guru's kitchen chooses the meal that leaves no one out. Fourth, a word from the Guru Granth Sahib itself. In a hymn of Guru Nanak, at Ang twelve eighty-nine, the Guru says, in paraphrase, that fools argue about flesh and meat while knowing nothing of meditation and spiritual wisdom. Some readers take it as a warning not to make food the measure of holiness. Others read it alongside their own vegetarian practice and find no conflict. The hymn turns the attention from the plate to the heart that eats from it. The code draws one line about what goes on the plate. The hymn asks about the one eating. Eat mindfully.
screen: `THE LINE: NO KUTHA.` · `VEGETARIAN, OR NOT: BOTH KEEP THE CODE.` · `LANGAR LEAVES NO ONE OUT.` · `FROM THE PLATE TO THE HEART.` · then, large: `EAT MINDFULLY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: eat mindfully. If you have something to eat or drink nearby, take it now; a sip of water will do. Settle, and breathe. Look at it first. Think of the hands it passed through on the way to you: a farmer, a driver, a cook. Then take one small bite, or one sip, and slow down. Notice the taste, the texture, the warmth or the cool. If you pray, you can remember the Giver as you eat. If not, just let the food have your full attention until the bell. The bell holds the time.

Food and the code. The code forbids kutha, ritually slaughtered meat, and leaves vegetarianism open; some Sikhs are vegetarian, others are not, and the langar is meatless so all can share. Today's word.
Your line: eat mindfully. Today, at one meal, put the phone away and taste the first three bites. Day one thousand two hundred ninety-one.

notes: Kutha is rendered as 'meat from an animal killed by ritual slaughter', following the index. The Sikh Rehat Maryada's own wording specifies the Muslim method of slaughter; the script does not name it, to avoid framing a neighbor tradition as a foil. A Keeper should decide whether to name it and how.
The two explanations of the prohibition (refusing another community's rite; refusing empty ritual) are attributed to 'some' and 'others'; please confirm both are held and fairly put.
'Many keep a vegetarian kitchen' follows the index ('many Sikhs are vegetarian'); 'some groups within the panth hold to it strictly' names no group; confirm.
'The langar serves vegetarian food' is stated generally; please confirm the wording and whether exceptions should be noted.

The Ang 1289 hymn of Guru Nanak (Malar ki Var, salok 'fools argue about flesh and meat') is paraphrased, not quoted; please confirm the Ang reference and the paraphrase, and that both readings given are fair.
Original: ਕੁੱਠਾ; confirm spelling and pronunciation.
